crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work covers the use of a researcher's existing papers, reports, datasets, and prior proposals as source material for new grant applications. The practice includes identifying reusable claims, methods, and results, then adapting them to a new funder's requirements. For AI researchers, this means turning a personal or institutional corpus into structured building blocks that can be searched and reassembled. The goal is to reduce repetitive writing while keeping the new proposal accurate and specific to the call.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a searchable index of past documents, usually built with embeddings that map text passages to vectors. A retrieval system pulls relevant passages from that index when a new proposal topic is entered. A language model then generates draft text conditioned on those retrieved passages. This setup can run on a single research workstation for small corpora or on cloud infrastructure for larger institutional libraries.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Past work is first broken into claims, such as findings, methods, or limitations, and each claim is linked to its source paper. When a researcher starts a new proposal, the system retrieves claims that match the funder's topic and uses them to draft sections like background, objectives, and approach. The site's extraction of 10,767 claims from research works illustrates the scale at which this decomposition can operate. Draft text includes links to the original papers rather than to a third-party search tool, so reviewers can verify the source.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on ownership, attribution, and accuracy. Past work may be co-authored, institutionally owned, or under publisher copyright, so reuse in a proposal requires checking what can be copied or paraphrased. A key risk is that a language model may generate text that overstates a past result or misattributes a claim, so teams keep a provenance record linking each drafted sentence to its source claim. Funder rules on originality and prior disclosure also shape how much past language can be reused.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Future systems are likely to assemble full proposal drafts from a researcher's publication history with less manual prompting, while still flagging which sentences need human review. Funder-specific templates and scoring rubrics may be built into the drafting process, so the output matches the call's structure more closely. Verification of claims against the original papers will become more automatic, reducing the time spent checking citations. The human role will shift from writing first drafts to editing, validating, and tailoring the generated text.
